title: 4D printing of multi-state pH-responsive microstructures - Nature Communications
byline: Tran; H B Duc; Mainik; Philipp; Gomez Melo; Santiago; Flórido Martins; Lilliana; Schwarz; Ulrich S; Spiegel; Christoph A; Blasco; Eva
html:
Abstract

Deep eutectic systems (DESs) are emerging as highly versatile functional materials for 3D printing, particularly in multiphoton 3D laser printing (MPLP), a powerful technique for the fabrication of complex microstructures with high spatial resolution. Here, we present a versatile strategy for the fabrication of multi-state pH-responsive microactuators based on polymerizable DESs using MPLP. By incorporating vinyl phosphonic acid and vinyl imidazole as functional monomers, respectively, we establish two actively responsive DESs that exhibit antagonistic swelling behavior across the pH range while maintaining excellent printability. The printed 3D microstructures show pronounced and reversible pH-responsive actuation with high cycling stability. Combining both materials within single architectures enables multi-state and bidirectional actuation beyond conventional bilayer systems. Complex actuator geometries further demonstrate the versatility of the platform. A hyperelastic theory implemented in a finite element framework can predict the experimentally observed actuation patterns. These results highlight the potential of polymerizable DESs as a new material platform for advanced microscale soft robotic, sensing, and adaptive systems.

Introduction

Deep eutectic systems (DESs), also known as deep eutectic solvents, have recently attracted significant attention as promising platform in various areas including electrochemistry, catalytic reaction design or development of soft functional materials1,2,3,4,5. They are especially attractive due to their high sustainability and an important element of green chemistry6,7. The characteristic feature of DESs is their liquid state at room temperature, resulting from the strong intermolecular interaction of their respective components. Furthermore, DESs offer several additional advantages including low vapor pressure, high thermal stability, adjustable polarity and a strong ability to solubilize ionic and molecular species, establishing them as a broader class of functional liquids with highly tunable properties6,8,9,10. Beyond their role as solvents, the ion-rich nature of DESs enables strong coordination and electrostatic interactions supporting the design of functional polymer networks and materials5,8,11,12,13. In this context, the subclass of polymerizable DESs (DESs with components bearing polymerizable functionalities) has proven to be an excellent basis for the design of soft polymeric materials13,14.

Recently, polymerizable DESs have gained attention as materials for three-dimensional (3D) printing15,16. Their photoreactivity and physical tunability render them an ideal ink platform for light-based 3D printing, allowing to achieve 3D architectures of highest degree of structural precision and print fidelity11,17,18. Especially at the macroscale, light-based 3D printing of polymerizable DESs has enabled the fabrication of complex, stimuli-responsive, and ionically functional components with programmable mechanical behavior16,19,20. Despite promising macroscale developments, the implementation of this material class for microscale 3D printing remains largely unexplored. In this context, multiphoton 3D laser printing (MPLP) has emerged as an ideal fabrication technology, as it enables the direct writing of complex 3D architectures with submicrometer resolution21,22,23,24,25. Our group has, for the first time, presented the use of polymerizable DESs for MPLP and demonstrated outstanding printability with only a minimal, tunable amount of a covalent multifunctional crosslinker5. Accordingly, the DES-based ink design strategy enabled facile access to low-crosslinked materials for the fabrication of 3D micro- and mesoscale architectures with soft, elastic properties. Considering the restricting effects of high degrees of crosslinking on polymer network mobility, such a material design strategy appears particularly attractive for the realization of complex microactuators capable of responding to external stimuli26,27,28,29.

Stimuli-responsive microactuators have attracted considerable interest owing to their ability to convert external stimuli into programmable mechanical motion30,31. Among the materials explored for this purpose, hydrogels are particularly attractive due to their ability to undergo pronounced and controllable volume changes in response to external stimuli like temperature or pH32,33,34,35. Thermoresponsive polymers such as poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAAm)-based hydrogels represent one of the most extensively studied material systems. Their capability to reversibly change structural volumes on the basis of exploiting their lower critical solution temperature (LCST) has enabled the realization of a broad range of temperature-responsive microactuators fabricated by MPLP27,28,36,37. Apart from thermoresponsive systems, pH-responsive hydrogels have attracted attention, particularly for applications in soft robotics and biomedicine38,39,40,41,42,43,44. Their actuation originates from reversible protonation and deprotonation of the pH-responsive units within the polymer network, leading to an accumulation of charges in the respective networks. The resulting alterations in charge density generate osmotic pressure differences that drive reversible phase transition changes45,46,47,48,49,50,51,52. In MPLP, pH responsive hydrogel systems are typically based on polyacrylic acid as an acidic component or dimethylaminoethyl methacrylate as a basic component22,34,46,51,53,54,55,56,57,58,59. While these hydrogel-based materials have enabled elegant demonstrations of microscale actuation, the realization of more complex MPLP-fabricated actuator architectures remains challenging. Current designs predominantly rely on single-material systems exploiting greyscale approaches or bilayer architectures featuring one active hydrogel component beside a passive static component, restricting the number of accessible actuation states and final actuator complexity27,28,34. Moreover, hydrogel-based materials often suffer from narrow processing windows and high sensitivity towards fabrication parameters. Furthermore, the need for moderate to high amounts of covalent crosslinker in reported ink formulations typically limits actuation at the expense of suitable printing performance. In this context, polymerizable DESs provide a promising material platform to overcome these limitations for stimulus-responsive microactuator design. The inherent tunability of DES-based systems allows precise adjustment of chemical and physical material properties, supporting material compatibility in multi-material fabrication strategies. Exploiting these advantages may enable the realization of more complex pH-responsive bilayer microactuators comprising multiple active materials as demonstrated at the macroscale by extrusion-based fabrication techniques60, while maintaining the high-resolution features of light-based techniques.

Herein, we present a versatile strategy for fabricating multi-state pH-responsive microactuators by leveraging polymerizable deep eutectic systems (Fig. 1a). By printing multi-material structures using two actively responsive DES-based materials, bidirectional and multi-state actuation is achieved, controlled solely by pH. To achieve this, we extend the pH-responsive material palette beyond conventional systems by introducing vinyl phosphonic acid as an acidic component and vinyl imidazole as a basic counterpart, and formulating them into polymerizable DES-based MPLP inks. This combination not only ensures excellent microprinting performance but also enables multi-material structures to exhibit multi-state actuation (Fig. 1b). We demonstrated these advanced actuation features by a range of complex 4D microarchitectures, whose actuation patterns can be predicted by computer simulations based on hyperelasticity implemented in a finite element framework.

The deep eutectic systems are formed through coordination interactions between the monomers and metal cations (M = Li⁺, Zn²⁺). Bottom: Multi-material bilayer fabrication of pH-responsive microstructures via sequential MPLP. The bilayers consist of a vinyl imidazole-based network (Im, blue) and a vinyl phosphonic acid-based network (PO₃H₂, orange) integrated within a single architecture. b Working principle of pH-responsive actuation in printed bilayer microstructures. Changes in pH induce reversible protonation and deprotonation of the functional groups, resulting in asymmetric swelling and deswelling of the individual layers and opposite bending directions under acidic and basic conditions.

Results

pH-responsive printable systems based on deep eutectic systems

To realize the targeted multi-state pH-responsive actuation behavior, two materials with antagonistic responses to pH changes were required: one system that is activated under acidic conditions, as well as one system that responds under basic conditions, such that the two materials undergo opposing transitions across the pH range. This antagonistic design principle enables differential actuation of printed structural elements in response to the same pH stimulus, which is a prerequisite for subsequent multi-state shape morphing. To this aim, we selected vinyl phosphonic acid and vinyl imidazole as the base monomers for the two targeted pH-responsive materials (Fig. 2a). Vinyl phosphonic acid is a Brønsted acid (pKa,1 ≈ 2.0, pKa,2 ≈ 7.7) whose phosphonic acid groups undergo progressive deprotonation with increasing pH. Within the material’s network, this deprotonation generates fixed negative charges along the polymer backbone, leading to electrostatic repulsion and osmotic pressure buildup, which drives network expansion. Accordingly, the phosphonic acid-based material responds under basic conditions, where the degree of ionisation and swelling increases with pH. Vinyl imidazole, by contrast, bears a Brønsted-basic imidazole ring (pKa ≈ 6.0) that becomes protonated under acidic conditions. Protonation introduces positive charges into the imidazole-based network, again generating electrostatic repulsion and osmotic swelling. However, in this case, the response is triggered at low pH. The imidazole-based network will therefore respond antagonistically to the phosphonic acid-based counterpart, forming the basis for the envisioned multi-state actuation strategy.

Swelling degrees were calculated with respect to 3D model dimensions (20 µm x 20 µm pillars). Values represent a single measurement per condition (n = 1); no error bars are shown. c Optical microscope images of DES-Im (blue) and DES-PO₃H₂ (orange) pillar arrays after pH changes. At lower pH values, DES-PO₃H₂ pillars remain unchanged, while the swelling of the DES-Im pillars yields a minus-sign (-) pattern. At higher pH values, swelling of the DES-PO₃H₂ pillars produces a plus-sign (+) pattern, whereas the DES-Im structures show no response. Scalebar: 20 μm.

Next, we aimed to translate this material design concept into a processable material platform for MPLP. For this purpose, we exploited a design strategy based on polymerizable deep eutectic systems (DES), targeting opposed pH-responsive features. To this end, we prepared two DESs: a phosphonic acid-based DES (DES-PO3H2) and an imidazole-based counterpart (DES-Im). For the preparation of DES-PO₃H₂, vinyl phosphonic acid was mixed with zinc chloride, yielding a stable, homogeneous, and highly viscous liquid upon cooling to room temperature. The eutectic formation is attributed to strong coordination interactions between the phosphonic acid groups and Zn²⁺ ions, as well as to hydrogen bonding contributions. For DES-Im, vinyl imidazole was combined with lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI). Similar to DES-PO3H2 a clear homogenous liquid was obtained at room temperature. ¹H NMR spectroscopy of both DES compared to their monomeric components revealed characteristic signal broadening consistent with increased viscosity and restricted molecular mobility, indicative of supramolecular interactions between the metal salts and the monomers (Fig. S1–4, Supplementary Information). IR spectroscopy further corroborated these findings: compared to the neat monomers, the DES spectra display broader absorption bands, reflecting the distribution of coordination within the supramolecular network (Fig. S5, Supplementary Information).

Subsequently, printing formulations (inks) suitable for MPLP were prepared by incorporating a suitable multiphoton photoinitiator and a multifunctional crosslinker into each DES (Fig. 2a). Each ink consisted of 91 wt% DES (DES-PO₃H₂ or DES-Im), 8 wt% poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate (PEGDA, Mₙ ≈ 700 g mol⁻¹) as covalent crosslinker and 1 wt% 7-diethylamino-3-thenoylcoumarin (DETC) as photoinitiator (section S2, Supplementary Information, for preparation details). The crosslinker content was kept lower than that used in conventional MPLP formulations for pH-responsive materials, to maximize stimuli-responsive swelling while maintaining sufficient mechanical integrity for handling and characterization of later printed microstructures. In contrast to conventional hydrogel inks, which contain a solvent as an inert diluent, the DES-based formulations used here are solvent-free, with the deep eutectic system itself constituting the liquid phase. Therefore, no water is present in the ink until the printed structures are exposed to an aqueous medium. The resulting inks exhibited good stability and processability, with no phase separation, precipitation, or degradation observed over storage periods of up to one month.

Following ink formulation, the printability of both DES-PO₃H₂ and DES-Im-based inks was systematically evaluated using a commercial MPLP device. The processing window was assessed by fabricating arrays of micropillars at laser powers ranging from 15 to 35 mW and scanning speeds ranging from 4000 to 28000 µm s⁻¹. Overall, the pillars of both DES-based inks exhibited smooth surfaces and no structural collapse or delamination. In contrast to conventional hydrogel-based responsive systems, which typically display narrow processing windows and high sensitivity to printing parameters, the DES-based formulations exhibited a large dynamic range, tolerating extensive variations in laser power and scanning speed. This behavior can be attributed to an efficient radical polymerization process during microprinting. Closer inspection of the fabricated pillars revealed for both DES-based inks optimal structural fidelity at a laser power of 30 mW and a scanning speed of 4000 µm s-1. To assess the mechanical properties of the two DES-based networks and their dependence on crosslinking density, nanoindentation measurements were performed on printed cylindrical micropillars (100 μm x 100 μm x 20 μm) fabricated at laser powers of 25 and 35 mW. For DES-Im, the reduced elastic modulus increased from 4.8 ± 0.7 MPa at 25 mW to 6.9 ± 0.5 MPa at 35 mW. DES-PO₃H₂ exhibited overall lower stiffness, with reduced elastic moduli of 0.9 ± 0.1 MPa and 1.1 ± 0.1 MPa at 25 and 35 mW, respectively. As expected, increasing the laser power and consequently the crosslinking density led to an increase in the reduced elastic modulus for both materials, an effect notably more pronounced for DES-Im, indicating a stronger dependence of its mechanical properties on crosslinking density (Fig. S15, Supplementary Information).
